hook: In fifteen eighteen, hundreds of people in one town danced for days.

blocks.narration: In fifteen eighteen, hundreds of people in one town danced for days. Many reportedly could not stop, even when they wanted to.
blocks.visual: Cinematic storybook illustration of a medieval square at dusk, a lone figure dancing on cobblestones, dramatic light

blocks.narration: It started in July in Strasbourg, then part of the Holy Roman Empire, when a woman began dancing alone in the street.
blocks.visual: Illustrated half-timbered houses, townspeople staring from doorways at the dancing woman

blocks.narration: She kept going for days. Within weeks, others had joined her. Some accounts put the number at hundreds of people.
blocks.visual: More figures join in a swirling crowd, faces exhausted, muted reds and sepia

blocks.narration: Local authorities made a strange decision. They believed more dancing would cure it, so they built a stage and hired musicians.
blocks.visual: Illustrated musicians with drums and pipes playing on a wooden stage above the crowd

blocks.narration: It only made things worse. Some reports claim dancers collapsed from exhaustion, though historians still debate how many actually died.
blocks.visual: Dancers slump against walls in dim torchlight, archival paper texture

blocks.narration: So what happened? A leading theory is mass psychogenic illness, a kind of stress-driven behavior that spreads through a community.
blocks.visual: A web of glowing threads connects anxious faces across the town

blocks.narration: Strasbourg had suffered famine, disease, and extreme hardship. Many people also believed in a curse tied to a saint.
blocks.visual: Illustrated empty grain stores and a shadowy shrine lit by candles

blocks.narration: Eventually the dancers were taken to a shrine, and the outbreak faded as mysteriously as it began. Comment your theory below.
blocks.visual: A procession winds toward a mountain shrine at dawn as the camera pulls back

captions.hook_line: In 1518, hundreds of people danced for days and couldn't stop 💃
captions.body: In July 1518 in Strasbourg, a woman began dancing in the street and others soon joined, with accounts reaching hundreds of people. Authorities even hired musicians. Historians often point to mass psychogenic illness under extreme stress.

youtube_title: The Town That Couldn't Stop Dancing
